item.title: Starlink spectrum deal boosts Musk plan to beat AT&T, T-Mobile, and Verizon
item.description:
Nationwide 800 MHz spectrum to help Starlink provide mobile coverage indoors.

SpaceX has a deal to purchase nationwide low-band spectrum licenses for a planned terrestrial mobile network that would complement the space-based Starlink cellular service.

SpaceX will buy up to 14 megahertz of spectrum in the 800 MHz bandfrom investment firm Grain Management, which bought the spectrum rights from T-Mobile earlier this year. T-Mobile had obtained the spectrum when it bought Sprint in 2020 and was required to sell the licenses under a merger condition imposed by the US government.

“This prime low-band spectrum addresses one of the key remaining technical gaps that will pave the way for Starlink Mobile to become a major mobile carrier in the US,”SpaceX said yesterday. SpaceX this week also received US approval to launch 15,000 satellites for an upgraded version of its mobile service that it says will be far more powerful than the current offering.

The 800 MHz spectrum licenses cover “approximately 100 percent of the US population,” the Federal Communications Commission said in a July 2026 orderapprovingGrain’s purchase of the T-Mobile licenses. While the licenses are nationwide, it’s not a huge amount of spectrum. It ranges from 4.85 megahertz to 14 megahertz depending on the county. The FCC said the 800 MHz spectrum can be used for terrestrial service, satellite-to-mobile service, or both.

SpaceX’s low-band purchase is in addition to 65 MHz of nationwide mid-band spectrum licenses it is buying from EchoStar. The FCC approved that $17 billion purchase in May 2026.

“While Starlink Mobile’s global 2 GHz mid-band spectrum will provide high-bandwidth capacity in the United States, this new low-band spectrum will provide a coverage layer that ensures Starlink Mobile’s signal penetrates through obstacles, such as walls, and can provide service to customers’ devices even when they are in buildings. Critically, most existing mobile devices already support this underused band,” SpaceX said.

SpaceX’s spectrum deal is likely to be approved by the FCC, but it could face opposition from small carriers. The Rural Wireless Associationopposed EchoStar’s spectrum salesto AT&T and SpaceX, saying the deals “continue the troubling pattern of spectrum aggregation that disadvantages rural wireless providers.” Across all carriers in the US, there isabout 1.1 GHzof licensed spectrum allocated to mobile operators, withthe big threeholding dominant spectrum portfolios.

SpaceX has beenclaiming for monthsthat Starlink Mobile will eventually offer better service than AT&T, T-Mobile, and Verizon. SpaceX previously focused on partnering with carriers and providing them with satellite coverage for dead spots in their terrestrial networks. Stock prices for AT&T, T-Mobile, Verizon, and satellite company AST SpaceMobile fell sharply today in response to SpaceX’s spectrum deal.

SpaceX’spartner for mobile servicein the US is T-Mobile, and the space company leased 10 MHz of nationwide mid-band spectrum from T-Mobile as part of that deal. With this week’s Grain deal, SpaceX is buying former T-Mobile spectrum in order to compete against the giant wireless carrier.

CEO Elon Musksaid in Augustthat Starlink would deploy many small base stations instead of “expensive and difficult-to-locate large cellular base stations.” He said the Starlink broadband antennas on the roofs of houses and businesses can help provide connectivity to cellphones.

SpaceX yesterdaysubmitted a filingthat asks the FCC to approve the low-band purchase. It said the deployment “will rely on radios feeding sectorized antennas on towers, rooftops, and other structures, configured to provide reliable signal coverage and meaningful broadband service. The propagation characteristics of 800 MHz (long-range coverage, strong performance against terrain and clutter, and superior building penetration) make this paired low-band spectrum an efficient coverage layer for markets of all sizes and densities, including areas where higher-frequency networks cannot serve.”

SpaceX has launched 650 Direct-to-Device satellites for its current mobile service and plans tolaunch up to 15,000next-generation satellites for a more powerful version. The FCCapproved the 15,000-satellite applicationon Tuesday.

“The V2 Starlink Mobile satellites will deliver more than 100 times the bandwidth of our current generation, bringing high-speed service directly to unmodified devices anywhere in the world,” SpaceX said yesterday. “Additionally, the FCC authorized the full range of backhaul bands (in Ka/V/E/W) used by Starlink’s V3 broadband satellites, enabling them to operate with the existing Starlink gateway network.”

SpaceX said that once it deploys all its spectrum and launches next-generation satellites, it will be able to offer US residents “a reliable service indoors, outdoors, in cellular dead zones, and everywhere in between.” SpaceX previously told the Canadian government in afilingthat it “will begin launching its next-generation Starlink direct-to-device satellites with service beginning by late 2027,” and launch “thousands more satellites” by the end of 2028.

Terms of the SpaceX/Grain spectrum deal were not disclosed. Grain originally obtained the spectrum from T-Mobile in a swap that included cash and other spectrum licenses. Specifically, T-Mobile sold its 800 MHz spectrum licenses to Grain for $2.9 billion and Grain’s 600 MHz spectrum licenses that consist of 10 MHz in 212 counties covering approximately 15 percent of the US population.

“The 800 MHz licenses that Grain is acquiring (817–824 MHz paired with 862–869 MHz)—a valuable source of paired, broadband-ready, low-band spectrum—have been underutilized in recent years,” the FCC said in its approval of the cash-and-spectrum swap.

Dish was previously given the first option to buy the 800 MHz spectrum under a merger condition imposed by the US Department of Justice on T-Mobile’s purchase of Sprint. Dishdeclined the optionto buy it for $3.59 billion, and the offerexpiredin 2024, forcing T-Mobile to find a new buyer.

AT&T, T-Mobile, and Verizon are trying to counter SpaceX’s moves into mobile by pooling spectrum for a new joint venture focused on using satellite to cover dead zones in terrestrial networks. The big three carriersfinalized the joint venture agreementlast week, saying it will give other satellite operators a better chance to compete.

The venture will “improve the application and utilization of valuable and scarce nationally licensed spectrum resources,” the carriers said. They said they plan industry-wide device compatibility through a “standards-based approach to development involving operating system providers, mobile app developers and original equipment manufacturers.”

Existing carrier-satellite agreements will remain in place, and the three big carriers “can continue connectivity efforts independently,” the press release said. Meanwhile, anFCC planannounced this week could auction 25 MHz of mid-band spectrum for use in terrestrial and satellite networks.

The FCC alsoproposedrule changes that would allow 482 MHz of spectrum to be used for satellite-to-mobile service. This would be an expansion of the Supplemental Coverage from Space (SCS) framework in which terrestrial wireless spectrum is made available for satellite use.

item.title: Your artwork could be featured in the next Debian release
item.description:
Debian Linux has put a call out for artist submissions for its next release: Forky.

The Debian Linux project has opened a call for community artwork submissions ahead of the release of the upcomingForky(Debian 14). If you think you’ve got the artistic chops, your art could appear on the boot screens, login prompts, and desktop wallpapers of millions of users. The submission deadline is November 26.

Continuing Debian’s community-driven ethos, the artwork submission process mirrors that of previous releases. The artwork must feel distinctively “Debian,” integrate cleanly without the need for core software patching, and remain visually appealing for the long term.

Elise Couper’s “Ceratopsian”theme was chosen as the winning default for Debian 13Trixie. For anyone who might not be up on the latest from the Toy Story franchise, the release names echo character names from the animated films.Trixiewas a triceratops introduced inToy Story 3, hence the “Ceratopsian” wink in the winning submission. It makes sense that the next version of Debian continues this trend with Forky, a character introduced in the franchise’s fourth entry. The Debian team cautions against overly busy designs that may cause user fatigue, but if anyone can successfully incorporateForky’s googly eyesinto the design somehow, know that you’d at least win the contest formyDebian desktop wallpaper.

Debian celebrated its 33rd anniversary in August 2026 and continues to position itself as the “universal operating system,” with support and compatibility stretching acrossdifferent hardware architectures. Debian’s latest point release, Trixie 13.7, arrived on September 12, 2026. Forky (Debian 14) is now in the later stages of its development cycle, with the artwork selection process marking one of the final boxes to be checked before the release is made available. Interested artists can review the submission requirementson the Debian Wiki.

item.title: AI disqualification yields new Nikon Small World in Motion winner
item.description:
New winner is Nguyen Nam Nhat of Vietnam for video of a roundworm and single-celled Dileptus.

Last monthwe coveredthe winner of Nikon’s Small World in Motion video: Ning Xu of Tsinghua University in China, whose video captured tiny cilia beating in the airways of a child with a rare respiratory disorder. Butallegations surfacedabout Xu’suse of AIwhile making the video. Nikon launched an investigation and concluded that Xu’s entry did not comply with competition rules. The new winner is Nguyen Nam Nhat of Vietnam with a video of a tiny roundworm and a single-celled organism (above).

According to aBBC report,some researchers expressed concern that Xu’s video had structural abnormalities and that cell features appeared and disappeared in a way one would not see in actual cellular biology. Others spotted what looked like AI watermarks embedded within the source files. Xu said he used AI “to distinguish and visualize features in the reconstructed grayscale images”; however, he denied that AI was used “to generate the experimental movie, the cilia, or their motion.”

Founded in 2011, the Nikon Small World in Motion competition is a spinoff of the company’s Small World Photomicrography Competition, which has been around since 1974. Both are meant “to showcase the beauty and complexity of things seen through the light microscope”—one through still photographs, the other through photovideography, taking advantage of all the technological advances that now allow users to make movies or time-lapse images through the microscope.

The other winners also moved up a notch with Xu’s disqualification. Benedikt Pleyer of Bavaria, Germany, placed second with a video of jellyfish larvae suspended in water droplets; Andrew Moore of Howard Hughes Medical Institute in the US placed third with a video of synchronized cell division in neighboring cells; Patrick Hickey of Hypha Research Ltd. in Edinburgh, Scotland, placed fourth with a video of the dynamics of mitochondria and chloroplasts in Turtle Vine leaf cells; and Igor Adameyko placed fifth with a video of a tiny, colorful sea slug (Cyerce kikutarobabai) on the move.

Here is Nikon’s full statement:

After thoroughly re-evaluating the video and supporting materials and consulting with members of our judging panel, Nikon has determined that the winning video did not comply with the competition rules regarding generative AI. Nikon has adjusted the competition rankings on our website to reflect this decision.

This decision is based solely on the submitted video’s eligibility under the rules outlined for this competition. It should not be interpreted as a judgment of the entrant’s professional reputation, scientific contributions, or intent.

Advances in imaging and artificial intelligence continue to evolve rapidly, creating new challenges for organizations across many fields. This event has shown the need for Nikon Small World and Nikon Small World in Motion to revisit rules and evaluation procedures for future competition entries.

The Nikon Small World and Nikon Small World in Motion competitions celebrate excellence in imaging, both scientific and artistic in nature. We value the integrity of each image and video selected to appear in our winning galleries, and remain committed to upholding the standards of excellence that have defined this competition.

item.title: PC shipments fall 20.1 percent in “sharpest decline” since Q1 2023
item.description:
“The current decline may be just the beginning of a new downward cycle.”

PC shipments saw a steep drop of about 20 percent in Q3 2026, analysts reported this week.

The industry saw its “sharpest decline since “Q1 2023,” Omdia said in an announcement toady. Global shipments of laptops, desktops, and workstations fell 21.2 percent year over year (YoY) to 58.1 million devices, the analyst said.

Desktop PC shipments (including desktop workstations) decreased 23.5 percent to 11.7 million units, and laptop shipments (including laptop workstations) declined 20.6 percent to 46.4 million, per Omdia.

IDC shared similar findings. The analyst said this week that PC shipments fell 20.1 percent YoY to 62.7 million units, compared to 78.5 million in Q3 2025.

The industry also shipped 9.1 percent fewer PCs in Q3 2026 than it did in Q2 2026, when 68.2 million units shipped, per IDC.

The 20.1 percent YoY decline is the biggest drop that the IDC has ever recorded during a year’s third quarter, the IDC said, perPCMag.

The drop in shipments is also notable considering that Q3 PC shipments usually surpass Q2’s numbers.

“If looking at all quarters, then we have seen other quarters in recent years with larger declines, such as 2022 Q4, which was -28.2 percent, and 2023 Q1, which was -28.7 percent. Both were coming off pandemic highs,” Jitesh Ubrani, research director for consumer devices at IDC, told PCMag.

In its announcement this week, IDC said that many PC vendors and sales channels stocked up on PC shipments earlier in the year in anticipation of memory price hikes. That meant minimal demand remained during Q3.

“[Sales] channels are now worried about carrying too much inventory into a market where high prices are suppressing demand,” Ubrani said in a statement.

“That could translate into promotions and some short-term relief for consumers, but we don’t expect pricing anywhere near what it was a year ago. Prices will remain elevated. With macro conditions worsening, the risk is that the outlook for the next few quarters gets worse before it gets better.”

IDC said that it expects PC prices to decrease “only modestly and briefly.”

Omdia research director Ishan Dutt said the Q3 drop “comes as no surprise.”

“The impact of upstream component cost increases has now fully worked its way through to end-market pricing, with consumers and IT decision-makers responding accordingly. On the supply side, vendors and their ODM partners began scaling back production in [Q3], while channel partners continued working through elevated inventory levels,” he said in a statement.

Since 2025, surging demand for HBM and server DRAM for AI workloads has led to limited manufacturing capacity for consumer devices, like consumer PCs,smartphones,andgaming consoles. Memoryand storagenowrepresent nearly 40 percent of the bill of materialsfor PC manufacturing, but it’s typically 15 percent, per Ben Yeh, principal analyst at Omdia. Meanwhile, PC prices have increased “more than fourfold,” he said, adding:

Although PC vendors have raised prices multiple times over the past few quarters, these increases have yet to fully offset the impact. These pressures are expected to persist, and the current decline may be just the beginning of a new downward cycle.

Omdia expects PC shipments to decline 24 percent YoY next quarter and then 7 percent in 2027.

Last week, executives from Micron and Samsung indicated the components shortages couldcontinue through 2028.

“Alongside continued increases in memory and storage prices, shortages of processors, graphics cards, and numerous IC components have made supply chain and inventory management more difficult for PC vendors,” Omdia said.

item.title: Outrage grows as CDC reportedly poised to fund “unethical” vaccine trial
item.description:
CDC allocated $1.6M for study on alleged harms of hepatitis B vaccine.

Outrage has erupted among health experts over news that the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention is still eager to fund a widely condemned vaccine trial that would expose newborns in Guinea-Bissau to hepatitis B, putting them at high risk of a lifelong infection, which can lead to liver cirrhosis, liver cancer, and premature death.

The trial was suspended in Januaryafter its unethical design came to light and drew international outcry. Although the trial is still halted, staff of the CDC director’s office told the agency’s budget office in late September to set aside $1.6 million to fund the trial, according toa report by Rolling Stone. The money was to be pulled from funding for the CDC’s global health security programs, which might otherwise go toward efforts like combating the Ebola outbreak currently raging in the Democratic Republic of the Congo.

The Department of Health and Human Services, which oversees the CDC, did not respond to a request for comment from Ars Technica.

If the trial moves forward, it would be funded by the US but run by Danish researchers, who have separately been accused of misconduct. In December, the CDC announced the award of an unsolicited grant for $1.6 million to a research group at the University of Southern Denmark, led by married couple Christine Stabell Benn and Peter Aaby. The pair have produced numerous studies that have been promoted by anti-vaccine advocates, drawingconcern and criticismfrom researchers. Stabell Benn and Aaby are currently under investigation by Danish authorities over allegations of“falsification” and “scientific misconduct”related to previous vaccine research.

In January, amid criticism of the trial, officials in Guinea-Bissau said they had suspended the research, saying ethical and technical reviews of the trial’s design were ongoing. “There has been no sufficient coordination in order to take a final decision regarding the study,” Quinhin Nantote, the minister of public health for Guinea-Bissau, said at the time. “Faced with this situation, we decided to suspend it.”

The trial intends to enroll 14,000 newborns in Guinea-Bissau, half of which would get a newborn dose of hepatitis B vaccine, while the other half would not. The aim is to try to find alleged vaccine harms from the newborn dose—despite the fact that the newborn dose has been proven safe and effective after decades of global use and is the current standard of care.

Guinea-Bissau has a high burden of hepatitis B in its population, and newborns who are not vaccinated at birth are at risk of acquiring a chronic, life-threatening infection. Authorities in Guinea-Bissau want newborns to be vaccinated and intend to begin universally administering birth doses in 2028. The country, which experienced a coup in November 2025, does not currently have the resources or infrastructure to provide those routine vaccinations.

Stabell Benn and Aaby have argued that the trial is not unethical because newborns in Guinea-Bissau are currently not routinely given a dose of hepatitis B vaccine at birth. But outside experts point to ethical guidelines, such as theDeclaration of Helsinki, which requires trials to provide the “best proven intervention”—which is a birth dose of hepatitis B vaccine—regardless of whatever the current standard is in the country hosting the trial. Placebos may only be used when there is no proven intervention or there is “compelling and scientifically sound methodological reasons” to withhold a proven intervention.

In a scathing rebuke in February,the World Health Organizationlaid out a bullet-point list of “why withholding the vaccine is unethical.” The WHO notes that the entire premise of the trial is based on “hypothetical safety outcomes without sufficient credible evidence,” which don’t justify putting newborns at risk. The agency also blasted Stabell Benn and Aaby’s defense of the trial, saying: “Resource constraints cannot be used to justify withholding proven care in a research study involving people. Ethical obligations require minimizing risk and ensuring a prospect of benefit for participants.”

According to the Rolling Stone report, the trial’s design has been revised to now ask mothers if they are infected with hepatitis B—which can pass from mother to infant during birth—and test a small fraction of them for the infection. But the changes have not eased concerns that having an unvaccinated group as part of the trial is fundamentally unethical.

For now, the trial is still on hold, pending final authorization from Guinea-Bissau officials. But the CDC, under anti-vaccine Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., appears eager to move forward with it once it is approved. Researchers at the University of Southern Denmark, where Stabell Benn and Aaby are based, recently granted approval to the revised trial design,CIDRAP reported Thursday. Professor Jakob Grauslund, dean of the university’s faculty of health sciences, also told the outlet that the “relevant ethics committee in Guinea-Bissau” has signed off on the trial and that government authorization is the final step.

“[T]he study cannot begin until the necessary national authorization has been obtained,” Grauslund said.

Nonprofit advocacy group Stand Up for Science vowed to block the trial. “We stopped this unethical study the first time and we’ll do it again,” Colette Delawalla, the group’s CEO and founder, said ina statement. “This is a gross violation of human rights and the use of bad science against some of the most vulnerable people in the world.”

item.title: AI coding agents generate more code, but not more software
item.description:
Study finds coding efficiency gains get “absorbed” by human review “bottleneck.”

Anyone who has even tangentially associated with computer programming knows that modern AI coding assistants and agentscan be incredibly efficient at generating huge amounts of functional code. But coders making use of those tools alsoknow better than to trust the accuracy of that code, meaningsubstantial effort needs to be spentreviewing any AI-generated output.

A recent studyof actual coding practices across hundreds of firms finds that human code review forms a significant “bottleneck” for the overall efficiency of AI coding tools, resulting in “little evidence that firms increase software output or reduce employment” by using them. Any efficiency increased during the actual coding phase, the study authors find, is “absorbed by downstream constraints in the production process”; as “the code review process significantly increases in length, pull requests are more likely to require revisions, and reviewers leave more comments.”

To come to these conclusions, Harvard University researchers Fiona Chen and James Stratton made use of aggregated analytics data fromJellyfish, which measures the granular output of engineering teams. That data encompasses 300 million individual “work events” (e.g., commits and pull requests) and issue management software data across more than 700,000 employees at over 700 relevant software development firms from 2021 through March of 2026.

To assess the impact of AI tools on these firms, the researchers used a mix of directly measured AI usage and analyses of GitHub activity to determine when each company started introducing either AI coding assistants (which can help auto-complete code primarily authored by humans) and/or AI coding agents (which primarily write and submit code autonomously based on prompts) into their workflows. The researchers then perform some complicated math to determine a “difference of differences” regression on key variables both before and after the introduction of these tools at different points in time across different organizations.

In terms of raw code being produced, the results are clear and stark. The introduction of AI coding agents at a firm leads to a 30 percent increase in total lines of code generated, a 20 percent rise in the number of total commits, and a 23 percent increase in pull requests on average, the researchers write. But all that extra code doesn’t translate directly into improved software output on the firm level. On the contrary, the resolution rate for Issues and Epics (i.e. wholesale software features) tracked by tools like Jira did not change in a statistically significant way after AI tools were introduced (the researchers also found no “compositional shift” in the size or complexity of those Jira-tracked issues across the AI introduction).

The reason for that discrepancy can be found directly in the code review process, which takes markedly longer on average after the introduction of AI coding agents. Overall, the average “review process” time between a pull request getting submitted and it being merged into the codebase balloons 49 percent on average after AI agents are introduced. That effect can be seen in more granular data, too, with “the share of pull requests with changes requested nearly doubl[ing], and the number of comments per pull request increas[ing] by 35%” following the AI agent shift, the researchers write.

In response to this change, the researchers found a 14 percent increase in the share of workers performing code reviews after AI agents’ introduction. They also write that they “cannot attribute significant employment changes to AI” after looking at total active workers across Jellyfish and cross-referencing with LinkedIn data at those firms.

While AI could also theoretically help with this review process, the researchers found that, so far, that impact has been marginal. Although 80 percent of measured firms used some form of AI code review by March 2026, AI agents were only responsible for 23.3 percent of all review comments and 10.8 percent of all pull requests, suggesting humans were still responsible for the vast majority of this work.

AI agents are still a relatively new part of the coding world, of course, and there have been significant updates and upgrades to their output even since this study’s March 2026 data cutoff. And while 95 percent of firms in the study have implemented AI coding agents by this point, many are doubtlessly still going through a learning process regarding when and how to best deploy them. These kinds of “coding time versus review time” trade-offs could improve as software engineering teams gain more experience with the pros and cons of siccing an AI agent on particular coding problems.

For now, though, letting AI write your code looks like a double-edged sword, with increases in coding speed counteracted by similar increases in human code review time and effort. It’s the kind of result that makes us wonder if the considerable time and expense to get AI coding agents working is really worth it for most companies.

item.title: What’s been driving Hawaii’s lava fountains?
item.description:
Before the lava fountains started, the ground was expanding by half a meter a day.

In most cases, hotspot-driven volcanism is relatively sedate, with lava flowing down mountainsides slowly enough that people can walk out of its way. But in a number of locations—Mount Etna, Hawaii, Iceland—lava gets expelled in dramatic fountains that can reach several hundred meters in height.

Right now, we’re not sure what powers them. However, thanks to a recent set of eruptions at the Kilauea volcano, we have some of the best documentation yet of erupting lava fountains. In a recent edition of Science, researchers from the US Geological Survey describe what we’ve seen and compare it with what we might expect based on our best ideas about what powers these fountains of molten rock.

With three active volcanic regions that engage in fountaining, there has been a steady flow of dramatic videos of red-hot molten rock spouting from the Earth. But Kilauea has had only three fountaining episodes since 1823, even though it’s the youngest and most active volcano in Hawaii. That activity has led to intensive study, and we have a good idea of the volcano’s structure. Previous work has identified a couple of lava residues within a few kilometers of the surface, and the volcano had 35 separate data-gathering stations set up on Kilauea, including “seismic, infrasound, geodetic, gas, and visual and thermal cameras.”

Followinga major eruption in 2018that partly drained one of the underground lava reservoirs, there were indications that it was being steadily refilled. Starting in 2019, however, the refill accelerated, and the local peak inflated at a rate of more than 22 cm a year. Then, in 2023, that doubled to 57 cm a year, and spread to a nearby caldera.

In 2024, a large series of earthquakes accompanied the opening of a vent, and a 900-meter-long fissure opened, sending fountains as high as 160 meters into the sky over the course of 13 hours. Less than a day after that subsided, a second eruption followed. As of last month, 52 additional fountain eruptions had occurred, the most violent of which spewed lava over 400 meters into the air.

What have we learned from all of this?

Perhaps the most significant finding was that we could predict when a fountaining eruption was likely to happen. Each eruption caused rapid deflation of the summit of Kilauea and was followed by the relatively slow refilling of the Halemaʻumaʻu magma reservoir.

The USGS recognized that consecutive eruptions occurred when the summit tilt reached similar levels. While the precise tilt that was associated with eruptions tended downward over time, the difference between consecutive eruptions was relatively small. This pattern ultimately helped the organization issue alerts when eruptions were likely to occur, which was especially useful because there were no clear seismic signals immediately before fountains restarted.

What have the eruptions told us about the mechanism that drives fountain formation?

One leading idea is that pressure within a magma reservoir keeps water mixed with other materials until it reaches a shallow enough depth to exit as steam. That fragments the magma, which allows it to ascend more rapidly, which allows more steam to escape, and so on until there’s a jet of material near the surface. The alternative posits that things are driven by the release of carbon dioxide from the magma, which forms a magma/gas “foam” at the roof of the magma chamber. Once this reaches a critical point, the gas escapes, driving magma with it until the supply in the magma chamber is exhausted.

The new data doesn’t provide a clear picture. It clearly doesn’t favor the formation of a carbon dioxide foam, because the levels of the gas remained low throughout the eruption cycle. Sulfur dioxide levels rose during eruptions and dropped afterward, but remained high throughout the entire period. Levels of this chemical are associated with gases escaping from magma, so this implies that more of it goes on during eruptions, but it also occurs continuously between them.

So the evidence leans toward the steam-driven eruption model, but it’s unclear why a process that is occurring throughout the cycle suddenly triggers fountains when it rises a bit.

The other bit of information from the chemistry of the eruption is from magnesium oxide, which provides an indication of the temperature of the magma. It fluctuated throughout the eruption cycle, consistent with a cycle in which eruptions deplete a reservoir, which is then refilled with hot material. In contrast, other oxides rose over time, suggesting that the newly arriving material has a distinct chemical composition.

Despite the wealth of nearby sensors, the researchers acknowledged it would be nice to have more data. Sampling of gas levels is typically done at infrared wavelengths and, as you can probably imagine, there was a lot going on in the infrared during a fountaining eruption. And, because of the height of some of the fountaining, it wasn’t necessarily safe to install more monitoring hardware. One camera notablysacrificed itselfin order to bring us images of red-hot, semi-molten rock falling from the sky.

While Kilauea has proven itself as a spectacular lab for studying volcanic activity, it hasn’t yet proven ready to give up all its secrets.

Science, 2026. DOI:10.1126/science.aef2931(About DOIs).

]]>

item.title: NASA issues long-awaited call to industry for private space stations
item.description:
“We’ve made it clear that NASA will never give up its presence in low Earth orbit.”

NASA on Friday released a much-anticipated “request” to the US commercial space industry to develop private space stations that, as early as 2030, will succeed the International Space Station as a place for astronauts to live in low-Earth orbit.

In a cover letter accompanying the 360-page “request for proposals,” NASA stated its plan: “This will ensure NASA has a sustained human presence in LEO for crew members to perform science and exploration.” Several private companies that have worked for years on designing and developing such stations have been keen to learn exactly what capabilities NASA is seeking. These new documents finally provide some answers.

NASA’s solicitationcan be found here. Industry responses are due back to NASA on December 8. NASA said it plans to select “two or more” contractors in this phase of the competition, and intends to make a final decision in April.

“We’ve made it clear that NASA will never give up its presence in low Earth orbit,” NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman saidin a statementthat accompanied the release of the new documents. “We will continue to need a place to conduct research, develop technologies, train crews, and prepare for missions to the Moon and Mars. Commercial space stations may provide that capability while creating new opportunities for American industry and allowing NASA to concentrate more of our resources on the near-impossible missions ahead.”

Bidders for this funding phase will certainly include Axiom Space, Voyager Space, and Vast Space. Blue Origin won an earlier round of funding from NASA, but questions remain about the company’s commitment to the program. SpaceX appears unlikely to bid, at least for now. Phase 1 winners will be guaranteed at least $100 million.

Future phases of the contract will be worth billions. NASA said Phase 2 of this “Commercial LEO Destinations” competition, kicking off next year, will include funding for development and certification of space stations, and Phase 3 will include the purchase of at least four missions for NASA astronauts to the private space stations.

One of the most closely watched elements of the NASA request was its provisions for crewed transportation to the stations. In earlier discussions with potential space station providers, NASA had indicated it may leave acquiring transportation to the contractors—basically saying it was their responsibility to sell an end-to-end service to the space agency.

This is problematic because SpaceX has said it plans to retire the Crew Dragon spacecraft as soon as possible, and almost certainly when the International Space Station is deorbited in 2030 or 2032. SpaceX, which has the only operational US vehicle for such transportation, has not offered to sell seats to private space station operators. This led NASA,two weeks ago, to provide an additional $359 million to support Boeing’s ongoing efforts to certify its Starliner spacecraft for crewed missions to low-Earth orbit.

But in the new request for proposals (RFP), the space agency goes further in support of would-be space station operators. As part of their bids, contractors do not need to provide proof of a signed contract with Boeing (or another transportation provider), or even a letter of intent. NASA is even offering to “furnish” transportation for the first four NASA service missions to the private stations, likely meaning it will help broker deals between the private companies and Boeing.

Notably, in the new documents, NASA assigns an explicit price to crew and cargo missions. For 2030, it estimates a four-seat crew flight will cost $325 million, and a cargo flight $300 million. In offering to furnish these initial flights, NASA is taking a significant burden off private space station providers, which are already undertaking a challenging task in constructing, testing, and flying orbital space stations.

The potential bidders were still reviewing the lengthy proposal on Friday afternoon, but several offered their initial thoughts on the new NASA documents.

“The release of the RFP is an important milestone,” Marshall Smith, the chief executive of Voyager’s Starlab space station, said. “We appreciate that NASA has incorporated both industry and government feedback. We believe Starlab has the strongest business plan and technical solution to be America’s next space station and we look forward to competing.”

Axiom Space said it also welcomed the release of the final RFP.

“Our team is actively reviewing the RFP now and is energized for the next steps in the process,” an Axiom Space spokesperson said. “With years of experience executing human space flight missions and developing orbital hardware, we are confident the proposal we provide NASA will demonstrate that Axiom Space is the clear choice to meet NASA’s objectives in low-Earth orbit.”

Vast, too, said it was prepared to move forward with the competition.

“Vast looks forward to competing for the opportunity to build the commercial successor to the ISS,” a company spokesperson said. “We’re in final integration with Haven-1 and ready to keep building towards a multi-module station capable of supporting a continuous human presence.”

item.title: A Cray-1 supercomputer replica from 30 “obsolete” Mac Minis
item.description:
Stylish upcycling, with a retro flare, at Spain’s Museo de Historia de la Computación.

TheMuseo de Historia de la Computaciónin Spain has unveiled a 1:1 scale visual replica of the famousCray-1supercomputer from 1976. Instead of sourcing expensive, cutting-edge tech to run the system, the creative team powered the project with 30 2012-era Mac Minis. Developed over 18 months, the project serves as a 50th-anniversary tribute to the Cray-1 and Apple’s founding.

Mac Minis from over a decade ago might not seem like the obvious first choice for building a cluster supercomputer, but when networked together, the developers can orchestrate the 64 active processing cores into a combined 1.3 teraflops of performance in their most recent tests. The museum reportedly achieved 1.5 teraflops previously using all 70 available cores, prior to one node going offline. Benchmarks were obtained using a custom matrix-multiplication Python script. Five PCs are quad-core i7s, and the remaining 25 are dual-core i5 models. Except for two units from 2014, the rest of the array dates to 2012.

The replica is a valuable tool for museum-goers to understand the shifts in computer architecture since 1976. The original Cray-1 used vector processing, applying a single instruction to multiple data elements simultaneously, whereas the replica distributes work across independent processors in a parallel cluster. The peak theoretical performance of the original Cray-1 was approximately 160 megaflops. What was originally a purpose-built research machine has been re-created with consumer hardware that’s vastly more capable than the machine that inspired it.

Rather than opting for a more standard Linux distribution, the team found thatmacOS Mojave (10.14)met their project needs by harnessing macOS’s built-in support forMPI(Message Passing Interface), the software layer that allows all the nodes in the cluster to pass tasks to one another.

Guests at theMuseo de Historia de la Computacióncan watch in real time as the system runs matrix algorithms, mapping the scale of system performance from a single core to the full suite running in parallel.

Combining 30 consumer PCs into an operational cluster wasn’t the only engineering challenge the team faced. If you’ve ever stepped inside a server room, or, like me, foolishly installed one in your own basement, you know that fan cooling can beloud. The museum team used passive convection cooling via a steel rack chassis and aluminum tray mounts for each Mac Mini. Compared to the roaring thunder of a modern data center, this cluster is nearly inaudible.

The secret to the near-silence comes from vertical mounting. The PCs’ vertical orientation, combined with the steel chassis and aluminum trays, allows the tower to act as a natural thermal chimney. Hot air rises through the structure and out of the top grills without the need for added mechanical fans. According to the museum, the only noticeable noise inside the Cray-1 replica comes from two gigabit Ethernet switches at the base of the unit that register between 30–33 decibels, though the team plans to replace them with silent models. The fully assembled replica is said to make so little audible sound that you have to get right up next to the tower to be able to hear anything. While exact dB  measurements from inside the exhibit weren’t available, each individual PC is stated to produce12–15 dBA of noiseat idle.

To manage this quiet giant, designers built a custom terminal that looks straight out of a Cold War control room. The team combined elements of theDEC VT05andProcessor Technology Sol-20 Terminal Computerdesigns of the 1970s, even incorporating an analog control panel, with future plans to add original lamps from anIBM System/3. One master Mac Mini resides in the terminal and serves to direct all the other cluster nodes.

The original design had planned for the terminal to feature CRT monitors for added authenticity, but modern flat Samsung displays eliminated the connectivity headaches that come from attempting to bridge different technological eras. Future design plans will see 3.5- and 5.25-inch floppy drives mounted to the underside of the desk, and a 3D-printed shell will encase the keyboard to mimic the look of the classicHP 250 design.

The Cray-1 team hopes to fill the currently empty second half of the tower through a crowdfunding campaign to secure 70–80 additionalM4 Mac Minis. The goal: create a cluster capable of ranking on theTOP500 supercomputerslist.

The replica is on permanent display in the museum, alongside two unused authenticCray CX1systems. TheMuseo de Historia de la Computaciónoffers guided tours on Saturdays from 11:30 am to 2 pm. Additional project information can be found on themuseum website.

item.title: Ukraine’s drones knock out AI data center belonging to “Russia’s Google”
item.description:
One damaged data center has supercomputers used for training Yandex’s AI model.

Ukrainian drone strikes have knocked out two of five data centers belonging to the Russian tech giant Yandex. The damage has left Yandex, known as “Russia’s Google” because it operates the country’s most popular search engine, struggling to maintain its AI chatbot and other online services.

The Ukrainian drones struck Yandex data centers in the Sasovo and Kaluga regions of Russia on October 8 and October 9,according to Reuters. Those actions came as a direct response to aRussian drone strike campaign targeting Ukraine’s data centers, which has disrupted mobile phone and Internet services for thousands of Ukrainians since late September.

“We continue to respond to Russia’s attacks on Ukraine, and we’re doing so with high precision,” said Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyyin a poston X. “Another data center was hit as well—our symmetrical response.”

The Ukrainian company Firepoint said its FP-1 one-way attack drones were involved in the latest strike on the Kaluga data center that is Yandex’s largest such facility, Reuters reported. The first Ukrainian attack targeted Yandex’s Sasovo data center that houses two of the company’s three supercomputers used for training the company’s YandexGPT AI model.

Yandex said no employees were hurt but acknowledged disruptions to some services. Russian users reported problems accessing media websites and popular apps for the Ivi video streaming platform, the digital banking service T-Bank and the state-owned Russian Railways, according to the independentRussian news publication Meduza.

Other impacted Russian services included a dating app, a real estate aggregator, a self-publishing book platform and the website of the most successful professional soccer club in the Russian Premier League, according to Reuters.

Targeting data centers is just the latest example of them becoming wartime targets in 2026. After the United States and Israel attacked Iran in February, Iranian dronesknocked out multiple Amazon data centersin Bahrain and the United Arab Emirates.

But Russia has been regularly launching mass missile and drone attacks against Ukraine’s cities, targeting power grid infrastructure, transportation hubs and even residential apartment buildings since Russian President Vladimir Putin first launched his full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

Ukraine has recently been grappling with a shortage of interceptor weapons capable of shooting down Russian missiles and jet-powered drones. But the Ukrainian military has also gradually ramped up its own medium-range and long-range drone strike campaign in response to Russian attacks.

Ukraine’s drone strikes have focused on Russian military bases and supply lines,Russian-linked shipping in the Sea of Azovand Black Sea, and Russian energy infrastructure such as oil refineries. In the summer of 2026, Ukraine also targeted multiple warehouses belonging to the Russian companies Wildberries and Ozon, which are Russia’s Amazon equivalents.

In a sign of the potentially widening war, coordinated aerial and sea drone strikessank two commercial ships in the Black Seawithin the exclusive economic zones of NATO member countries Romania and Bulgaria on October 5 and October 6. Ukraine’s president Zelenskyy attributed those attacks to Russia.

item.title: Neanderthal wooden tools from Spain found preserved in stone
item.description:
Dissolved rock precipitated around the tools, which then decayed.

The Stone Age owes its name to tools that survived to our time. The material early humans worked with most, though, was probably wood because it is so much easier to process. Unfortunately, we know very little about Paleolithic woodwork because wood rots relatively quickly. But at Abric Romaní, a rock shelter in Capellades, west of Barcelona, mineral-rich water coated wooden Neanderthal tools in a limestone-like crust. When wood rotted away, it left behind hollow molds that faithfully reflect its shape.

In a recent Science Advances study, a team of Spanish archaeologists has cataloged 597 wooden remains from Neanderthal living areas dating from 62,000 to 40,000 years ago. They found spears, digging sticks, bark trays, parts of shelters, and a club unlike anything seen before, suggesting Neanderthals were likely much more than just Homo sapiens’ dumber cousins.

The oldest wooden artifacts we have are mostly weapons. They include spears from a German town called Schöningen, a spear tip from Clacton-on-Sea in England, and the spear found alongside an elephant skeleton in Lehringen, Germany. Most came from waterlogged sediments, where a lack of oxygen slowed decay.

The spears mostly give us information about how Neanderthals hunted. The findings at Abric Romaní are different because the finds come from a place where Neanderthals lived, slept, cooked, and made tools over the course of some 20,000 years.

“We have a sample of wooden tools for different subsistence activities, not only hunting,” says M. Gema Chacón, an archaeologist at the Catalan Institute of Human Paleoecology and Social Evolution (IPHES-CERCA) and co-author of the study. Because wood turns up in level after level, it shows that woodworking was routine for Neanderthals rather than an occasional one-off.

The shelter sits at the foot of a cliff of travertine, a limestone laid down by calcium-rich spring water. As that water dripped across the shelter floor, calcium carbonate settled on anything lying around—logs, leaves, pine cones, and Neanderthal tools. Sealed inside the crust, the wood slowly decomposed, leaving hollow molds. These are perfect negatives of the original objects, sometimes so detailed that the outlines of wood cells are visible under a microscope.

Abric Romaní has been explored continuously since 1983, so the team has had time to develop a method for excavating objects that are essentially empty space. Each find is outlined, mapped, and photographed, and restoration specialists consolidate the fragile crust. “Then we open very carefully one part of the object,” Chacón explains.

In the past, the team filled the hollows with resin or plaster to get a positive cast. “Now all the wooden remains are printed in 3D,” Chacón says. The molds are digitized with 3D scanning and photogrammetry, and the 3D-printed copies are used both for research and museum displays.

Most of the 597 remains turned out to be natural trunks, fallen branches, and lots of firewood, mostly Scots pine. Only 13 objects were made or modified by Neanderthals. “The morphology of these 13 tools is impossible to find in nature,” says Chacón.

Four shallow trays made of juniper bark, the largest 55 by 20 centimeters, were found near hearths. They may have been used to carry food or scoop embers, much like the bark dishes called coolamons used by Aboriginal Australians. Crossed poles over a thick hearth may be the remains of a tripod, possibly for processing food. A branchless pole more than five meters long was found in the innermost part of the shelter.

That pole fits a pattern seen in every level dug so far. Along the back wall, Neanderthals kept a row of small hearths, around 50 centimeters across and spaced a meter or so apart, with almost no debris around them. Chacón suspects these were sleeping hearths. “This gives you illumination and also protects you from possible carnivores or other animals that could attack the group,” she says. The team thinks the pole leaned against the wall to form a windbreak or simple hut, and experiments showed five meters is about the length such a structure needs.

The shelter’s busy end included large, overlapping hearths surrounded by animal bones, stone-knapping debris, and firewood. That’s where food was prepared, tools were made, and, the team thinks, meals were shared.

But there were also weapons.

The team found a pointed stick and two spears lying close to the antlered skulls of red deer. The best-preserved spear is 2.45 meters long. Chacón says a cast of its point shows an impact fracture identical to those on spears used by Aboriginal Australians. That kind of damage happens when a point strikes bone or something similarly hard. The most surprising find, though, was a club.

The club was carved from a single piece of wood, with a 16-centimeter handle and a pointed, roughly triangular head about 14 centimeters tall. Where the two meet, there is an abrupt right-angle step that may have kept the hand from slipping. The only earlier object hypothesized to be a club has been found in Kalambo Falls in Zambia and is roughly 400,000 years old. According to Chacón, nothing quite like the Romaní club has turned up anywhere.

Anthropologists have observed and documented hunter-gatherer groups over the last couple of centuries and found they used similar clubs to kill game at close range, fight, and sometimes as symbols of social standing. “But when it comes to this club it’s true that we are not sure,” Chacón admits. The club was found in a living area, next to bones, stone tools, and a hearth, so the team hypothesizes it’s been used for everyday work rather than ceremony.

The choice of materials suggests Neanderthals knew their wood. Scots pine is easy to work and dries quickly, so tools were cheap to make and replace. Juniper’s fibrous bark suited the trays. Firewood tended to be dry wood, while tools were made from fresh wood. “When they went to look for wood, it was like when they went to look for stone; they knew exactly what they wanted to make,” says Chacón. “This implies not only planning, but a bit of complexity in the brain to organize your activities.”

That fits a broader shift, as evidence has piled up that Neanderthals twisted fibers into cord, made symbolic objects, and interbred with our species. “Neanderthals are no longer perceived as Homo sapiens’ dumb cousins,” Chacón says. She suggested that the Abric Romaní tools may offer a new perspective to interpret finds at other sites.

“To study all these types of tools properly, you need a lot of time and budget,” Chacón says. Neanderthal tools from Abric Romaní were first described in the 1990s, so it took decades for the team to identify and catalog them. This makes her concerned that insufficient time and funds might have cost us missing similar discoveries elsewhere. “I hear from colleagues telling me ‘perhaps we found something that we thought was wood, we excavated it, we took pictures, but we didn’t keep it,’” she says. “Now they say perhaps it could be a tool.”

Science Advances, 2026. DOI:10.1126/sciadv.aeh2287
